transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

I’ve started going out of my way to avoid driving or being in cars, and it’s really taking over my life. It has gotten so bad that it's shrinking my whole world, and I realized I need help to figure out why I can't seem to move past this.
Can you tell me more about what specifically happens when you're in a car or think about driving that makes you want to avoid it?

If I hear tires screech or see headlights, I'll suddenly feel like I'm right back in the crash—pinned in the car and smelling gasoline while my heart races. Even as a passenger, I'm constantly on edge, staring at the mirrors and watching other drivers like they're about to hit us. To avoid that panic, I plan my whole life around staying off highways and only driving on back roads during daylight.
Do you experience these flashbacks or memories of the crash at any other times, such as when you're not in a car or thinking about driving?

Yes, they can happen completely out of nowhere, even when I'm not thinking about driving. If I hear tires screeching outside or see headlights coming toward me, I'm suddenly right back in that pinned car smelling gasoline. My heart just takes off like it's happening all over again, no matter where I am.
Can you estimate how often these flashbacks or memories of the crash occur in a typical week, and have you noticed any decrease or increase in their frequency over time?

I'm not really sure of the exact number of times a week it happens because it's so unpredictable and depends on when I run into triggers. But I can say they haven't really let up or decreased at all since the crash happened a little over two years ago.
Have you also been experiencing any significant difficulty falling or staying asleep, or have disturbing dreams related to the crash?
Honestly, I haven't really had major issues with my sleep or nightmares related to the crash. For the most part, once I actually get to sleep, I tend to sleep okay.
Do you find yourself experiencing significant emotional distress, such as anxiety or fear, when you're reminded of the crash or when you try to talk about it with others?

Yes, absolutely—if I hear a sound like screeching tires, my heart starts racing and I feel that same intense panic of being trapped all over again. Also, when people try to talk to me about it or suggest I just get back on the road, I get really irritable and snap at them, or I'll just shut down the conversation completely.
Can you describe how your avoidance of driving or being in cars has affected your social life, work, or other important areas of your life?

I've had to turn down so many catering jobs that I've put my plans to expand my business on hold, which has really hurt my income. On top of that, I've pulled back from family gatherings and seeing friends because I refuse to carpool or drive far, so I feel incredibly isolated. My whole world has just shrunk so much and it’s deeply frustrating.
Do you often find yourself having difficulty concentrating or feeling constantly on guard, even when you're not thinking about the car crash or driving?

Yes, my brain feels foggy a lot of the time, and I'll find myself staring into the fridge or reading the same recipe line over and over because I just can't concentrate. As for being on guard, it is definitely most intense when I'm in a car watching the mirrors and other drivers, but that constant tension and mental fatigue absolutely carry over into my day-to-day routine.
Can you tell me more about what you mean by feeling 'on guard' in your day-to-day routine, and how that affects your daily life and interactions with others?

Whenever I’m in a car, even as a passenger, I’m completely glued to the road and the mirrors, watching every other driver like they’re about to hit us. This constant, intense vigilance makes me so tense and distracted that I can’t even relax enough to hold or finish a normal conversation with the person next to me.

You mentioned feeling on guard and watching other drivers intensely when you're in a car, but can you tell me if you also experience this heightened sense of alertness or vigilance in situations unrelated to driving, such as when you're at home or in a quiet, safe environment?

No, I don't really feel that same level of alertness when I'm safe at home or in other quiet environments. That intense, on-guard feeling is really specifically tied to being in a car or on the road, where I'm constantly watching the mirrors and other drivers.
Do you often feel an exaggerated startle response, such as jumping or having a strong reaction to sudden noises, even when they're not related to cars or driving?

I don't really experience a strong startle response or jumpiness to general, everyday noises unrelated to cars. It's really just when it comes to traffic or driving-related situations that I get extremely tense and hyper-alert.
Have you tried to confront or gradually expose yourself to the situations or stimuli you're avoiding, such as driving or being in cars, and if so, how did you feel during and after those attempts?

There are times I force myself to drive home after a catering job, but I get so anxious that I end up speeding or running yellow lights just to get it over with. During those times, I am completely hypervigilant—constantly checking my mirrors and watching other cars, which makes me so tense that I can't even hold a conversation.

Can you describe a recent situation where you tried to confront your fear of driving, and how you felt during and after that attempt, to help me understand if your avoidance is primarily driven by fear of the crash itself or by other factors?

Just last week, I had to drive home from a late catering job, and I was so terrified of another crash that I was speeding and running yellow lights just to make the trip end faster. I was glued to my mirrors watching other cars, and when some oncoming headlights caught my eye, I had a sudden flashback of being pinned in the wreck all over again. By the time I finally got home, I was completely shaken, exhausted, and crying from the sheer panic of it all.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for the car crash, or do you have persistent negative thoughts about it?

Yes, I constantly think that if I hadn't taken that late job or if I'd just driven a little slower, the other driver might not have died and my life wouldn't be so messed up. Most days I walk around with this heavy mix of guilt and anger, feeling mad at myself for surviving and angry at the world for letting this ruin everything I'd been building.
Can you tell me more about how these feelings of guilt and self-blame have affected your daily life and relationships, and if you've noticed any patterns or triggers that make these feelings worse?

The guilt and anger have created an invisible wall between me and my loved ones, making me feel completely isolated and causing me to snap at them when they tell me to just "get back out there." These feelings get so much worse when I hear tires screech or see headlights coming toward me. They also flare up terribly whenever I am forced to drive home late from a catering job.
When you experience these flashbacks or feel like you're back in the crash, do you feel disconnected from your body or the world around you, like you're observing things from outside yourself?

No, I don't feel disconnected from my body or like I'm observing things from the outside. During those flashbacks, I actually feel everything very intensely in my body, like my heart racing and the physical panic of being trapped. It is more like I'm living through the actual sensory details, like smelling the gasoline, rather than feeling detached.

Can you help me understand if your avoidance of driving is more about the fear of having another crash or if it's also heavily influenced by the guilt and self-blame you feel about the original accident?

It is really a painful combination of both. When I'm in a car, I'm consumed by the terrifying fear of another crash, constantly watching other drivers as if they are about to hit us. At the same time, I torment myself with the guilt that if I had driven slower or turned down that late job, the other driver might still be alive, making the car a trigger for both intense fear and deep regret.
